cf.title: Add `tsmatch` JSONPath operator for granular Full Text Search

input.subject: Patch: Add tsmatch JSONPath operator for granular Full Text Search

verdict_reasoning: The goal is stated and plausible, but four design points need agreement on the list before code review. With no tsconfig, tsmatch reads default_text_search_config inside immutable jsonpath functions (standards-compat-1), and it resolves the config name with the caller's search_path (security-1). The unprefixed non-standard keywords and the dedicated predicate repeat concerns recorded in [P4] (prior-attempts-1, maintenance-fit-2). Demand is thin but does not stop the review alone (demand-1).

brief.title: Add tsmatch jsonpath operator for full text search in jsonb
brief.problem: Users cannot run full text search on one element of a nested jsonb document. jsonb_to_tsvector flattens all text into one vector, so a match cannot be tied to sibling keys in the same object. The workaround of unnesting with jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL is verbose and, per the author, uses much memory.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a boolean tsmatch predicate to the jsonpath grammar, modeled on like_regex, that tests a JSON string against a tsquery during path traversal. Optional tsconfig and tsqparser clauses, in any order, choose the text search configuration and the tsquery parser function. The compiled tsquery and config OID are cached in JsonPathExecContext for one execution; the predicate is not indexable beyond existing GIN path matching.
user_visible_surface: jsonpath predicate `@ tsmatch "query"`, usable in filter expressions with && and other conditions.
Optional jsonpath clause `tsconfig "regconfig"`; when omitted, default_text_search_config is used.
Optional jsonpath clause `tsqparser "mode"` with values "pl", "ph", "w"; omitted means to_tsquery.
New jsonpath keywords tsmatch, tsconfig, tsqparser, which change what jsonpath strings parse.
New jsonpath item type in the binary jsonpath format.
author_claims: tsmatch keeps the link between conditions in the same JSON object, which jsonb_to_tsvector loses.
It avoids the verbose SQL and memory cost of unnesting with jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL joins.
It follows the like_regex precedent, though the SQL/JSON standard defines no full text operator.
Caching gives compile-once behavior per execution and keeps prepared statements stable.
The author reports real-world need from his own work with JSON and full text search.
brief.thread_state: Chao Li reviewed v3 in detail (naming, grammar, context reuse across array items, error message bug), and Andrew gave off-list comments; v6 claims to address both. No one has replied to v4 through v6, and no committer has discussed the design.
unclear: The proposal does not say how dependence on default_text_search_config fits with jsonb_path_* and @@/@? being immutable, or with index expressions.
The benchmark files are attached, but the thread shows no numbers.
The default parser changed from plainto_tsquery in v1 to to_tsquery in v6, and the thread does not say why.
The proposal does not say how non-string values, such as numbers or objects, behave under tsmatch, or what lax and strict modes do.
The proposal does not say whether new keywords break existing jsonpath strings that use tsmatch, tsconfig or tsqparser as unquoted key names.
Chao Li's review message is truncated, so not all of his points are visible.

prior_attempts.title: Add jsonpath string method $.replace(from, to)
prior_attempts.who_objected: Andrew Dunstan, "David E(dot) Wheeler", Peter Eisentraut
prior_attempts.quote: The thing that bothers me about the original proposal is this: what if we add a new non-spec jsonpath method and then a new version of the spec adds a method with the same name, but not compatible with our method?
prior_attempts.reason: The thread does not state why the author withdrew the entry. David E. Wheeler noted that replace() is not in the SQL/JSON spec, and Andrew Dunstan objected that a future spec version could add an incompatible method with the same name, so he wanted non-spec method names prefixed or capitalized. Peter Eisentraut asked for a general way to call any suitable pg_proc function from jsonpath, and the author then began sketching that design instead.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: This adds a filter predicate with clauses for full text search, where [P4] added a string method. The naming concern and the request for a general function-call mechanism still apply, and the thread answers neither.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Reorganise jsonpath operators and methods"
prior_attempts.quote: The reordering of JsonPathItemType affects the binary on-disk compatibility of the jsonpath type, so we must not change it.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit 283a95da923605c1cc148155db2d865d0801b419.

The reordering of JsonPathItemType affects the binary on-disk
compatibility of the jsonpath type, so we must not change it.  Revert
for now and consider.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: [P1] reordered existing item types; this patch adds one. The addition is safe only if the new item type is appended without renumbering, and the patch prose does not say where it goes.

objections.title: Default tsconfig makes immutable jsonpath functions depend on a GUC
objections.failure_scenario: A user builds an expression index or generated column on jsonb_path_exists(doc, '$.c[*] ? (@.body tsmatch "run")'), which is allowed because the function is immutable. Another session or a restore runs with a different default_text_search_config. Index scans and fresh evaluation then disagree, and the user sees missing rows long after the change.
objections.argument: The doc hunk says an omitted tsconfig falls back to default_text_search_config. jsonb_path_*, @@ and @? are immutable, and the project already split off jsonb_path_*_tz so that timezone-dependent datetime behaviour does not leak into immutable functions. One-argument to_tsvector(text) is marked stable for the same reason. The proposal does not say which of these existing rules tsmatch follows.
objections.author_must_show: Will tsmatch without tsconfig be rejected in the immutable functions, as datetime is handled with the _tz variants, or how else does it keep them immutable?

critic.reasoning: The doc hunk says an omitted tsconfig uses default_text_search_config, and jsonb_path_exists, @? and @@ are immutable and allowed in index expressions. The thread does not address this, and the _tz split is existing practice for the same problem.

objections.title: Unprefixed non-standard jsonpath keywords, an objection raised before
objections.failure_scenario: A later SQL/JSON revision defines a full text predicate, or a keyword named tsmatch, with different syntax or semantics. Postgres then has to choose between breaking jsonpath values that users stored in tables, views and index expressions, or departing from the standard for good. The conflict appears only when someone implements the new standard.
objections.argument: In [P4], a non-standard jsonpath method from the same author drew the objection that the spec could later add an incompatible item with the same name. That entry also included a request for a general way to call pg_proc functions from jsonpath. This patch adds three bare keywords (tsmatch, tsconfig, tsqparser) and a dedicated item type, with no prefix and no general mechanism. Messages #1 and #8 point to like_regex as precedent, but like_regex is defined by the standard, and the thread does not discuss naming or how the patch fits the [P4] direction.
objections.author_must_show: Why should these non-standard keywords be unprefixed, and why is a dedicated predicate better than the general pg_proc call mechanism discussed for $.replace()?

critic.reasoning: like_regex is in the standard and tsmatch is not, so the like_regex model does not answer the naming concern. [P4] raised the same concern for a non-standard jsonpath addition, and the thread does not discuss prefixes or a general mechanism.

objections.title: Special-case tsearch hook instead of a general jsonpath function mechanism
objections.failure_scenario: Someone later adds a new tsquery parser function, or wants jsonpath to call another text function such as trigram similarity. Each case needs a new keyword, a new grammar rule, a new binary item and a new hard-coded mode string like "pl", "ph" or "w". Extensions cannot add their own.
objections.argument: The design maps short strings to four fixed tsquery functions inside jsonpath_exec.c, so jsonpath now carries a private copy of the tsearch parser list. In [P4], a reviewer asked for a general way to call suitable pg_proc functions from jsonpath instead of one-off methods, and the author started to sketch that design. This proposal returns to the one-off approach and does not say why the general mechanism was dropped. The accumulation test fails because ten such operators per release would be ten new grammar keywords.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a dedicated tsmatch predicate better than a general way for jsonpath to call a pg_proc function on a JSON value?

critic.reasoning: [P4] records a request for a general way to call pg_proc functions from jsonpath, in the same area and from the same author. The thread does not say why a dedicated predicate with hard-coded parser modes is preferred here.

objections.title: Config name resolved at run time from the caller's settings
objections.failure_scenario: An owner writes a row-level security policy with a tsmatch predicate. A user sets default_text_search_config, or sets search_path = myschema, pg_catalog with their own config named "english", so the stemming changes. The policy then returns a different result for that user, and nothing reports it.
objections.argument: The tsconfig string is kept as text in the jsonpath value and looked up when the path runs. The documentation says an omitted tsconfig falls back to the session's default_text_search_config. A regconfig argument to to_tsquery is resolved to an OID once, when the expression is created, so a stored expression always uses the same config. The proposal does not say how a jsonpath stored in a policy, view or index keeps one meaning for every caller.
objections.author_must_show: How does a tsmatch predicate stored in a policy or view get the same text search configuration whatever the caller's search_path and default_text_search_config?

critic.reasoning: The tsconfig name is stored as a string and resolved when the path runs, so the caller's search_path decides which configuration is used. That differs from a regconfig constant and goes beyond the immutability point, and the thread does not cover it.

objections.title: Demand rests on one author's workflow, and a workaround exists
objections.failure_scenario: The project adds a non-standard jsonpath predicate for a small group whose queries already work. Most users who need this today write a LATERAL query and apply `to_tsvector(...) @@ to_tsquery(...)`. If the memory claim does not hold, the main gain is shorter SQL, and the project carries the predicate for good.
objections.argument: The only stated demand is the author's own work (message #1). The thread has no -general or -bugs reports, no second user and no other database cited as having this. The one reviewer (message #5) reviewed the code without supporting the need. The memory cost of the workaround is claimed but not measured: the benchmark files are attached and no numbers appear in the thread.
objections.author_must_show: Which users besides the author have hit this, and do the attached benchmarks show the LATERAL workaround costing much more memory or time than tsmatch?

critic.reasoning: The only demand in the thread is the author's own work in message #1, and the one review covers code only. No benchmark numbers appear in the thread, so the memory claim is unmeasured.

other_surviving.title: New keywords may stop existing jsonpath strings parsing after upgrade
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An application keeps jsonpath values such as '$.tsconfig' or '$.items[*].tsmatch' in a table. pg_dump writes them as text. If the new keywords are not accepted as key names, the restore into the new server fails on that column, and queries using those paths raise syntax errors.
other_surviving.argument: The patch touches jsonpath_scan.l and jsonpath_gram.y and adds three keywords. Existing jsonpath keywords such as like_regex and starts stay usable as member names, but the proposal does not say whether the new keywords do the same. The patch also adds a new item type to the binary jsonpath format, and [P1] shows that changing JsonPathItemType order breaks on-disk compatibility.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Do '$.tsmatch', '$.tsconfig' and '$.tsqparser' still parse as member accessors, and is the new item type appended without renumbering existing ones?

critic.reasoning: Existing jsonpath keywords stay usable as member names only because the grammar lists them as key names. The material does not show that the three new keywords get the same treatment, and a failure would break restore of stored jsonpath text.

other_surviving.title: Default parser and mode names depart from existing text search conventions
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user writes '@.body tsmatch "fast car"', expecting the behaviour of text @@ text, which uses plainto_tsquery. Under v6 the default is to_tsquery, so the query string fails with a tsquery syntax error at run time, and only for rows that reach the predicate.
other_surviving.argument: v1 defaulted to plainto_tsquery (message #1) and v6 switched to to_tsquery (message #8) without giving a reason. The existing SQL operator text @@ text parses its right side with plainto_tsquery, so the jsonpath form would behave differently from the SQL form of the same idea. The mode codes "pl", "ph", "w" and the name tsqparser are a new naming scheme that does not match any existing function or option name.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should the jsonpath default differ from text @@ text, and why use "pl"/"ph"/"w" in place of names already used by the query functions?

critic.reasoning: text @@ text uses plainto_tsquery, and the thread gives no reason for the change from the v1 default to to_tsquery. The short mode codes have some support in the like_regex flag letters, but the default mismatch stands.

other_surviving.title: Existing SQL with jsonb_path_query and @@ already ties conditions together
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user needs Alice's comments that match "performance". They can write `exists (select 1 from jsonb_path_query(doc, '$.comments[*] ? (@.user == "Alice")') c where to_tsvector('english', c->>'body') @@ to_tsquery('english', 'performance'))`, which keeps the user and body link per element. Core then carries three new jsonpath keywords and a new binary item type to make this query shorter.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 names two workarounds, jsonb_to_tsvector and jsonb_array_elements with LATERAL. It does not consider using jsonb_path_query for the structural filter and the existing @@ operator for the text test. That split already gives per-element precision, so the job can be done today with more typing. The memory cost the author cites has no numbers in the thread, although tsmatch_bench files are attached to message #1.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What do the attached benchmarks show for tsmatch against jsonb_path_query plus to_tsvector @@ on the same documents, in time and memory?

critic.reasoning: jsonb_path_query for the structural filter plus to_tsvector @@ to_tsquery keeps the per-element link, so the alternative can do the job. The thread shows no numbers for the claimed memory cost, so the gain shown is shorter SQL.

refuted.title: Unprefixed non-standard keywords may collide with future SQL/JSON spellings
refuted.failure_scenario: A later SQL/JSON revision defines a full text predicate or a keyword named like tsmatch with other semantics. Postgres must then either break stored jsonpath values and application queries or stay incompatible with the standard.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states the standard defines no full text operator, so the patch claims three lowercase words in the jsonpath namespace. An earlier non-standard jsonpath method from the same author drew the objection that a future spec could add an incompatible method with the same name, and a reviewer asked for prefixed names or a general way to call pg_proc functions [P4]. The thread does not discuss either approach for this proposal.
refuted.author_must_show: Why are bare tsmatch, tsconfig and tsqparser keywords safer than a marked extension spelling or the general function-call mechanism suggested for the earlier replace() proposal?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1, which states the same naming concern with the same precedent and more thread detail.

refuted.title: Default text search config makes immutable jsonpath results session-dependent
refuted.failure_scenario: A user builds an expression index or check constraint on jsonb_path_exists(doc, '$.c[*] ? (@ tsmatch "run")') under default_text_search_config = 'english'. A restore, a session or a hot standby query with 'simple' gets different results than the stored index, so rows go missing without any error.
refuted.argument: jsonb_path_* and @@/@? are immutable, and the documentation hunk says tsmatch without tsconfig uses the session's default_text_search_config. The project already split timezone-dependent datetime handling into separate _tz variants for this reason. One-argument to_tsvector(text) is stable for the same reason, and only the regconfig form is immutable. The proposal does not say how tsmatch keeps the immutability promise.
refuted.author_must_show: Will tsmatch without an explicit tsconfig raise an error in the non-_tz functions, or how else will stored indexes and constraints stay correct when the setting differs?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The standby and check constraint cases are further examples of the same immutability problem.

refuted.title: New item type changes the stored binary jsonpath format
refuted.failure_scenario: A cluster stores jsonpath values in table columns and is pg_upgraded. If the new item type shifts existing JsonPathItemType values, stored values decode as the wrong operators after the upgrade, and users only notice when queries return wrong results.
refuted.argument: The jsonpath binary form is written to disk in user tables and is carried over unchanged by pg_upgrade. [P1] records a revert because reordering JsonPathItemType broke on-disk compatibility. v4 also changed binary serialization alignment (message #6), so the layout has moved during this patch's development. The proposal does not state that the new item is appended and leaves existing encodings untouched.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the patch append the new item type and leave every existing jsonpath encoding byte-identical, and do the tests check that?

critic.reasoning: The patch does not appear to reorder existing item types, and the v4 alignment fix seems to concern only the new item's own serialization. The remaining question is already asked in standards-compat-3.

refuted.title: Non-standard jsonpath keywords and item type become permanent
refuted.failure_scenario: A user stores jsonpath values that use tsmatch in a table column or a view. A later SQL/JSON revision defines a full text predicate with the same or similar spelling but different semantics. Postgres then has to keep both, or break stored values and dump/restore of those views.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says the SQL/JSON standard defines no full text operator, so tsmatch, tsconfig and tsqparser are Postgres-only words in a language that the standard owns. In [P4], an earlier non-standard jsonpath method from the same author drew the objection that the spec could later add an incompatible item with the same name, and the reviewer asked for non-spec names to be marked. [P1] records that JsonPathItemType values are part of the on-disk jsonpath format, so once the new item type is released it cannot be removed or renumbered. The proposal does not address either point.
refuted.author_must_show: How would a future standard full text predicate coexist with tsmatch, and why should these names not be marked as Postgres extensions?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. The added point from [P1], that a released item type cannot be removed, holds for any new jsonpath item.

refuted.title: Dependence on default_text_search_config inside immutable jsonpath functions
refuted.failure_scenario: A user creates an expression index or a generated column on jsonb_path_exists(doc, '... tsmatch "run"') with no tsconfig. A session with a different default_text_search_config then gets results that do not match the index. Nothing reports an error, and the user sees wrong answers only later.
refuted.argument: The documentation hunk says an omitted tsconfig falls back to the session setting, but jsonb_path_exists, jsonb_path_query and @?/@@ are immutable. Existing practice for jsonpath datetime handling is to raise an error in the non-_tz functions when a result would depend on the time zone setting. The proposal does not follow that practice and does not give a reason for leaving it.
refuted.author_must_show: How does tsmatch without tsconfig stay correct in immutable functions and index expressions, and why not follow the _tz approach used for datetime?

refuted.title: A one-off FTS predicate where a general function-call design was asked for
refuted.failure_scenario: tsmatch is committed with its own grammar, its own item type and hard-coded parser modes "pl", "ph" and "w". Later the project adds a general way to call pg_proc functions from jsonpath. tsmatch then remains a second path to the same to_tsquery and @@ code, and its item type cannot be removed from stored jsonpath values.
refuted.argument: In [P4], a committer asked for a general way to call suitable pg_proc functions from jsonpath instead of adding single non-standard methods, and the same author then started sketching that design. tsmatch is another single non-standard addition, with a mode flag mapped to four fixed parser functions. A general function-call facility would cover tsmatch and further text helpers with one mechanism. [P1] shows that jsonpath item types are part of the on-disk format, so a one-off item type is permanent.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should tsmatch go in as a dedicated predicate instead of as one use of a general jsonpath facility for calling pg_proc functions?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which makes the same general-mechanism argument from [P4].

refuted.title: Permanent jsonpath format and naming cost for a narrow gain
refuted.failure_scenario: A later SQL/JSON standard adds a full text predicate with different semantics. Postgres must then keep tsmatch, with its keywords and binary item type, next to the standard form. Every jsonpath user and maintainer carries this, while the gain goes only to tsmatch users.
refuted.argument: The patch adds a new item type to the binary jsonpath format, which cannot be removed or reordered later [P1]. In a similar non-standard jsonpath proposal by the same author, a reviewer warned that a future spec could add an incompatible item with the same name [P4]. Message #1 calls tsmatch modeled on like_regex, but like_regex is in the standard and tsmatch is not. With demand this thin, the trade-off is weak.
refuted.author_must_show: What demand justifies a permanent, non-standard jsonpath item type, and why does this not follow the more general pg_proc-call approach suggested for earlier non-standard jsonpath additions?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for naming and permanence, and of demand-1 for thin demand. It adds no separate cost that falls on users who do not use tsmatch.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a new item type to the binary jsonpath format, which is stored in user tables.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: see objection maintenance-fit-2: Special-case tsearch hook instead of a general jsonpath function mechanism

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: tsmatch, tsconfig and tsqparser are new jsonpath keywords that the SQL/JSON standard does not define.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: Immutable jsonb_path_* functions, usable in index expressions, would depend on default_text_search_config when tsconfig is omitted.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: Stored jsonpath text that uses the new words as key names must still parse on restore.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The tsconfig name is resolved at run time with the caller's search_path, which matters in policies and views.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: jsonpath gets a permanent non-standard predicate and a hard-coded list of tsquery parser modes.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: jsonb_path_query plus to_tsvector @@ to_tsquery already gives per-element matching in SQL.

questions: Will tsmatch without tsconfig raise an error in the immutable jsonpath functions, as datetime does outside the _tz variants, or how else do they stay immutable?
Why are tsmatch, tsconfig and tsqparser unprefixed, given the concern in [P4] that a later SQL/JSON revision could define the same names differently?
Why is a dedicated tsmatch predicate better than the general way to call pg_proc functions from jsonpath that was requested in [P4]?
Do '$.tsmatch', '$.tsconfig' and '$.tsqparser' still parse as member accessors, and is the new item type appended without renumbering existing ones?
What time and memory do the attached benchmarks show for tsmatch against jsonb_path_query plus to_tsvector @@ to_tsquery on the same documents?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the jsonpath grammar and binary format, with some knowledge of text search configuration lookup. The visible thread shows no committer discussing the design; the brief mentions only off-list comments.
committability.liability: The owner signs for three non-standard jsonpath keywords and a new on-disk item type that cannot be removed later. The owner also signs for the immutability of jsonpath functions that call text search code.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted six versions, responded to review, and moved the entry to a new CommitFest in October 2026.

priority.reason: The only demand shown is the author's own work, and existing SQL can do the job. The 33 KiB patch touches the jsonpath grammar, scanner, executor and binary format, and the immutability and naming points must be settled before that review is useful.

provisional_note: Without the code, three things could not be checked: where the new item type is added, whether the new keywords stay usable as key names, and how tsmatch treats non-string values in lax and strict modes. Only 3 of 8 messages were shown.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, Pavel Stehule, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to), and in v2 json_translate, which recursively replaces every value, including array elements, that exactly equals a given string with another string. The author meant it for mapping categorical or enum values deep inside a document, in the style of the Unix tr utility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrew Dunstan judged blind replacement of every instance of a string, regardless of context, to be a niche use and asked why it could not be an extension. Pavel Stehule suggested using JsonPath to say what to replace, and Peter Eisentraut pointed to json_transform in Oracle and the SQL standard draft, noting that json_transform and json_translate together might confuse users. The thread ends there, and the author later withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Blindly replacing every
instance of a single string regardless of context seems at best a niche
use. Is there any reason not to make this an extension?

precedents_retrieved.title: Add jsonpath string method $.replace(from, to)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, "David E(dot) Wheeler", Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a non-standard jsonpath string method, $.replace(from, to), which calls the internal implementation of the SQL replace() function on a JSON string value. The author planned more text methods, such as trim(), upper() and lower().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread does not state why the author withdrew the entry. David E. Wheeler noted that replace() is not in the SQL/JSON spec, and Andrew Dunstan objected that a future spec version could add an incompatible method with the same name, so he wanted non-spec method names prefixed or capitalized. Peter Eisentraut asked for a general way to call any suitable pg_proc function from jsonpath, and the author then began sketching that design instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The thing that bothers me about the original proposal
is this: what if we add a new non-spec jsonpath method and then a new
version of the spec adds a method with the same name, but not compatible
with our method?

precedents_retrieved.title: Flexible configuration for full-text search
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a CASE/WHEN/THEN/ELSE syntax to ALTER TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION ... ALTER MAPPING, so dictionary output can be combined with UNION, EXCEPT, INTERSECT and MAP BY, and the choice of dictionary can depend on whether another dictionary recognized the token. The comma-separated dictionary list stays for compatibility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Emre Hasegeli found the proposed syntax overly complicated and suggested a simpler grammar. The author agreed to rework the patch and also had a failing pg_dump binary upgrade test to fix. No new version came within three weeks, so Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Next version pending after three weeks, I am marking the patch as returned with feedback for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove 1MB size limit for tsvector
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the 1 MiB limit on tsvector by dropping the 20-bit `pos` field from WordEntry and storing offsets only at every 4th entry. Old-format tsvectors are converted on the fly when read, as hstore did, so pg_upgrade keeps working.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled for two months with questions unanswered, so Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback. The main open question was a regression of about 15% from on-the-fly conversion in the author's in-memory benchmark. Tomas Vondra would not accept that in-memory workloads can be ignored. The author argued that indexed searches do not read tsvectors, and Robert Haas pointed out that the RUM index he cited is not in core.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: That seems like a fairly significant regression, TBH.

precedents_retrieved.title: Flexible configuration for full-text search
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a CASE/WHEN/THEN/ELSE syntax to alter text search configuration, so a mapping can choose dictionaries by conditions on other dictionaries' output and combine outputs with UNION, EXCEPT, INTERSECT and MAP BY. The old comma-separated dictionary list stays for compatibility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback because the authors posted no updated patch after it stopped applying. Before that, the plan to move stopword filtering into separate dictionaries ran into backward compatibility problems. Tom Lane objected to breaking existing custom configurations, to forcing users to regenerate tsvector data, and to changing how stopwords count in phrase distances. The author asked for advice on the stopword counting problem and posted no new version.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think there should be a pretty high bar for forcing people to regenerate all that data when they haven't made any change of their own choice.

precedents_retrieved.title: Jsonb transform for pl/python
precedents_retrieved.summary: A set of extensions (jsonb_plpythonu, jsonb_plpython2u, jsonb_plpython3u) implementing a CREATE TRANSFORM for jsonb in PL/Python, mapping jsonb objects to dicts, arrays to lists, and numerics to Python Decimal via string conversion, and back. The transform works in both directions so functions can take and return jsonb as native Python values.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The reviewer objected that the third version turned unsupported Python objects such as set() into JSON strings instead of raising an error, asked for tests and errors for complex numbers and ranges, and reported that the tests failed on Python 3. The author sent no revised version after that review, and the commitfest manager returned the patch with feedback because it still needed work and had had no updates for more than a week.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So this still needs more work.. I am marking it as returned with
feedback as there has been no updates for more than 1 week.

precedents_retrieved.title: Collecting statistics about contents of JSONB columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a jsonb_typanalyze function that extracts every path from sampled JSONB documents and stores per-path statistics as an array of JSONB documents in pg_statistic under a new stakind. It also adds an "oprstat" procedure for operators such as ->> so the planner can derive statistics for expressions on JSONB columns.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tests showed ANALYZE becoming much slower: about 28 seconds against 120 ms on one data set, and over 2 hours or OOM on documents with about 850k distinct paths, because the patch loops over all sample rows once per path. The reviewers agreed the design of collecting statistics for every path in every JSONB column needs rethinking, for example by keeping only the most common paths or enabling the statistics per column. Nikita Glukhov posted optimizations and planned common-path collection, but in the last week of the commitfest the patch no longer applied and Greg Stark asked for a rebase.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: From these points, we can say that we should rethink our design to collect stats for all paths.

precedents_retrieved.title: introduce optimized linear search functions that return index of matching element
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds SIMD linear search functions, pg_lfind8_idx() and pg_lfind8_ge_idx(), that return the index of the first matching byte instead of true/false. It came from the radix tree work for lazy vacuum dead tuple storage, and this version also reworks the simd.h helpers it uses.
precedents_retrieved.objection: John Naylor judged that this level of abstraction is not right for the intended use case, the radix tree for lazy vacuum. He said some of the low-level simd.h improvements would be used later in that work, and he returned the entry with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I mentioned in the radix tree thread, I don't believe this level of
abstraction is appropriate for the intended use case.

roaster_notes.note: One objection only. The [P1] binary-format concern cannot be checked without the code, so it appears under prior attempts and is not raised as an objection.
Objections listed; nothing further from the standards and compatibility angle.
The proposal adds no WAL records, catalogs or wire protocol messages. Persistent state is limited to the binary jsonpath format and to indexes or constraints that use these functions.
Apart from the config lookup, the feature adds no new privilege surface. Text search configs have no ACL, and the query string comes from the caller, as with to_tsquery.
Committability: no committer has discussed the design on the list. Andrew's comments were off-list, so it is unknown who would own jsonpath grammar and tsearch coupling after commit.
Two objections raised; the existing SQL route can do the job, so the question is whether the convenience justifies the addition.
Two demand objections. Neither one shows that the user group is empty, so both are fixable with evidence.
